name: Manjula Pothos
description: A patented cultivar developed at the University of Florida, Manjula is one of the most beautiful and collectible pothos, prized for its wide, wavy, heart-shaped leaves with slightly ruffled edges and a swirling mix of green, silvery-grey, cream, and white variegation - often with speckles and patches unique to each leaf. Unlike Marble Queen's fine marbling, Manjula's variegation appears in broad, painterly sections, and its leaves tend to curl rather than lie flat, giving it a soft, sculptural look. It grows a bit more slowly and compactly than standard pothos, making it well suited to smaller hanging baskets or shelves. Care is the same easygoing pothos routine, with the usual variegated-plant caveat: it needs medium-to-bright indirect light to keep its creamy patches vivid and to avoid reverting toward green.
toxicity: Toxic to cats, dogs and horses. Chewing it causes mouth pain and swelling, drooling, vomiting and difficulty swallowing.

symptoms: Pain and swelling of the mouth, tongue and lips

careInstructions: Water when top 1-2 inches of soil are dry - typically weekly
Provide medium to bright indirect light to keep the cream and white variegation vivid
Avoid harsh direct sun, which scorches the pale sections
Prune to maintain shape and encourage bushier growth
Propagates easily in water or soil from stem cuttings below a node
Wipe the wavy leaves gently to remove dust
Fertilize every other month during spring and summer with diluted balanced fertilizer - skip winter
Grows slower and more compact than Golden Pothos - normal for this cultivar
commonProblems: Loss of variegation / reverting to green: Insufficient light - move to a brighter spot
Brown, crispy patches on cream areas: Sunburn from direct light or low humidity
Yellow leaves: Usually overwatering - allow soil to dry more between waterings
Brown leaf tips: Fluoride or chlorine sensitivity - use filtered water
Root rot: Overwatering or poor drainage

fertilizing.tip: Fertilize every other month during spring and summer with diluted balanced fertilizer - skip winter

whatsNormal: Variegated pothos grow more slowly than all-green ones and need brighter light to keep their color — in low light the pale patches shrink.
Older leaves yellow and drop over time, so leaves bunch toward the ends of the vines — prune stems back to keep it full.

propagation.tip: Cut below a node and root it in water or moist mix.

flags.note: Sources cover Epipremnum aureum, not the 'Manjula' cultivar. The brighter light for variegation follows NC State and Clemson's notes on variegated pothos.
Winter watering interval (10 days) is our estimate — the sources only say to reduce watering from fall to late winter.
Fertilizing monthly → every other month, matching the Pothos research (NC State, Wisconsin).
